newsitem.title: GERMANY: German banks brace for Deutsche Telekom listing.
newsitem.headline: German banks brace for Deutsche Telekom listing.

text.p: As German banks stopped taking orders for shares in Deutsche Telekom on Thursday, the financial community geared up for record turnover next week when Europe's biggest-ever stock offering will be launched.

Expecting record volumes from first-time trading in Telekom shares, bank employees are putting in overtime hours and German stock exchanges are bracing for extended trading hours next week to handle the additional business.
The German DAX of 30 leading shares is expected to continue rallying on Friday ahead of Deutsche Telekom's flotation.
"We hope our systems can deal with the volumes," said a Frankfurt banker, who asked not to be identified.

Banks around the country reported robust business ahead of the 2 p.m. deadline to place orders for shares of the German telecommunications giant that will begin trading on stock markets around the world for the first time on November 18.

The day marked one of the busiest periods after the rush of buy orders on November 6, the last day when people registered with Telekom's share information centre (AIF) were able to buy discounted shares and take advantage of other benefits.
"Buying interest was quite good right up to two o'clock but the rush of customers wasn't quite as strong as on November 6," said a spokesman for the savings bank Frankfurt Sparkasse.

Around three billion shares in Deutsche Telekom have been ordered by individual and institutional investors, which amounts to an oversubscription of the landmark offering of around five times, Telekom and banking sources said.

Facing overwhelming demand, Telekom topped up the issue by 20 percent earlier this week. It will now float up to 690 million shares, or around 25 percent of its capital. Another 30 million shares will be sold to Telekom employees.
The final share price will be set on Sunday, November 17. It is expected to be around 30 marks.

Marked by superlatives, Telekom's initial public offering, expected to have a volume of some $12 billion, will be Europe's largest-ever issue, potentially the third-largest in the world, and could mark the biggest-ever foreign listing in Tokyo.

It has whipped up such interest in Germany that nearly one and a half million individuals, many of them first time investors, tossed caution to the wind and cracked open piggy banks to take a chance on making a fortune on the stock market.

Even before the shares begin trading the government has declared the issue a success that could become a catalyst to broaden the base of equity holdings in Germany and create a more democratic ownership of industry.

"The Telekom share is the yardstick by which we will measure whether there could be demand for shares at all and whether a new kind of equity culture could be established in Germany," said Post Minister Wolfgang Boetsch.

With demand soaring beyond even the most optimistic predictions, German stock markets will extend trading hours next week and bank employees will work overtime as trade volumes are expected to make new records.

Commerzbank, Germany's third-largest commercial bank, will have 140 employees in the office on Sunday to process Telekom purchase orders. Deutsche Bank, Germany's biggest bank, plans to have 100 people at work over the weekend.

The stock exchange Deutsche Boerse AG has expanded its computer capacity. While the bourse on high-volume days in the past has dealt with up to 120,000 share orders, its computers are set to handle up to 600,000 transactions next Monday.
